vignette:
Marco's Reckoning

Marco Delgado was twenty-three years old when the bus collided with the overturned tanker truck on Interstate 95, just north of Jacksonville. He had been riding to a construction site where he worked summers before returning to his engineering program—a job his uncle had arranged, a way to stay connected to family and earn money. Marco sat in the middle section, near a window, listening to music through cheap earbuds. The driver had taken a route he didn't usually take, something about roadwork on the main highway. Marco remembered noticing the sky was cloudless and hot, the kind of Florida afternoon that felt like it would never end.

The impact came without warning. The bus lurched violently to the left, metal screaming against metal. Marco's body pitched sideways, his shoulder slamming into the window frame. For a moment that felt both instantaneous and eternal, he understood that something catastrophic was happening. The tanker had been lying on its side in the roadway—no one had seen it until it was too late. The bus driver had no time to brake. Sixteen people were on board. Three died at the scene. Two more in the hospital within days. Marco had broken ribs and a fractured collarbone. He had also been sitting directly behind an elderly woman named Mrs. Chen, who had been thrown into the aisle with tremendous force. He had seen her head strike the metal armrest. He had heard the sound. Later, he learned she was one of the three who died before the ambulances arrived.

The weeks after the accident unfolded in a fog of medical appointments and family concern. His mother had flown up from Miami and stayed in his apartment. His uncle stopped calling. Marco returned to his apartment alone in late August and tried to resume his life, but something fundamental had shifted in how he understood the world. He went back to his job as a QA engineer at a software firm in Jacksonville in September, sitting in a cubicle on the third floor of a downtown building, testing code for bugs and inconsistencies. His work required focus and precision—the same qualities that had once come naturally to him. But now, when colleagues would mention a car accident they'd seen on the news, or when someone casually referenced a crash, Marco felt something crack open inside his chest. His hands would shake. The office would seem to tilt. He found himself thinking about how different everything would be if he had taken a different bus that day, or if he had called in sick, or if the tanker truck had never been on that highway at all. These thoughts would consume him for hours, branching into elaborate scenarios where Mrs. Chen was still alive, where the driver had taken the main route, where he had never taken the job at all.

By October, Marco had begun avoiding the news entirely. He stopped watching television. He deleted news apps from his phone. When his roommate would turn on a program and a story about a transit accident or a highway incident appeared, Marco would leave the room abruptly, sometimes without explanation. He found himself increasingly uncomfortable around police—a patrol car pulling into the parking lot of his apartment complex would send him into a state of hypervigilance that could last for hours. He wasn't sure why exactly. The police had been kind at the scene. But something about their presence now felt like a threat he couldn't name.

What frightened Marco most was the conviction that had taken root in him: that he should have somehow protected Mrs. Chen, that his proximity to her created an obligation he had failed to meet. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that you could never truly know who or what would harm you, and that nothing good could happen to him anymore. The thought of returning to school felt impossible. The thought of getting close to anyone—romantically, or even in friendship—felt like exposing them to danger through association with him. At work, he had become quieter, less engaged. His manager had asked twice if everything was okay. Marco had said yes both times, but he could feel the erosion happening, the slow withdrawal from the life he had been building.

By late November, a year after the accident, Marco's mother called after not hearing from him for several days. Something in his voice alarmed her enough that she insisted he see someone. He sat in a therapist's office for the first time last week, hands folded in his lap, and spoke about the bus, about Mrs. Chen, about the weight of a guilt that belonged to no one but had attached itself to him anyway. He was terrified that talking about it would make it real in a way it hadn't been before. He was also, somewhere beneath the fear, hoping that someone might tell him that the future wasn't entirely foreclosed, that he hadn't somehow poisoned everything he touched by surviving.
